sections.text: It is not right to give up actions which are obligatory; and if they are misunderstood, it is the result of sheer ignorance.
To avoid an action through fear of physical suffering, because it is likely to be painful, is to act from passion, and the benefit of renunciation will not follow.
He who performs an obligatory action, because he believes it to be a duty which ought to be done, without any personal desire to do the act or to receive any return - such renunciation is Pure.

We had been discussing chapter 18, Moksha Sannyasa Yoga. The very title implies that liberation will only come from renunciation. In other words, something which we are holding on to is binding us.
If we let go of whatever is binding us, well be released. And as we have discussed many times before, this chapter is a summary of the entire Bhagavad Gitas teachings so far. All throughout these chapters which we had been discussing, there is one central theme: that either Sannyasa (renunciation) or Tyaga (abandonment) is the key to this liberation.
So the chapter opened with Arjunas question: what is Sannyasa and what is Tyaga? And Krishna explained that Kamyanam Karmanam Nyasa Iti Sannyasa -- giving up all the desire-prompted activity is Sannyasa, and Sarvakarma Phalatyagam -- giving up the desire for the fruits of actions is Tyaga. And then Krishna took up the theme of Tyaga as the most important thing because at our level, Sannyasa is probably not possible. Giving up all desire-prompted activities is probably not possible at our level because everything we are doing right now is prompted by some desire.
Even the things which I consider Im doing as community work or selfless activities -- when you go to the root cause of why youre doing it, there is some desire which is prompting you to do that. There are people who are involved in a lot of organizations which are community-activity based. We know theyre very active as long as they have a position -- president or chairperson or board member.
And suddenly they lose that position and the person disappears from that organization. All those were supposed to be selfless activities. It was helping the community, it was helping the people it was intended for, but it was not truly selfless for the person performing it.
It was not directly benefiting them in terms of monetary gain, but there was something which was feeding their ego. Bhagavan constantly says Tyaga is giving up attachment to the fruits of actions. And that is something which at our level we can understand and we can practice.
So he takes up the theme of Tyaga and says, there are philosophers who say that all actions should be given up. Because they say any action which you perform binds you to its results, whether good or bad. Good binds you to good results, bad binds you to bad results.
When youre bound by the good results, you want them to be repeated over and over and over again. I want to be successful again and again and again. I go to Las Vegas and experience beginners luck.
First time I go to the slot machine and win some money. So I think thats how it works. Next time also it should work the same way.
So we get bound by this good result. And then sometimes we lose our shirt in Las Vegas and want to avoid that. So we are bound by the results.
And therefore some philosophers, Bhagavan says, says all actions must be given up. You will never be bound by anything. But Bhagawan said, thats probably not possible for us anywhere.
Therefore, he says, I recommend the second opinion which says yajna dana, tapah should not be given up. Yajna the offerings, dana the charity and tapas the discipline, austerities, which is what at our level we can relate to it as what we do as yajna is all our efforts in this life is a yajna. All that we give back to this world as our results of our efforts is adana.
And whatever we do to discipline ourselves is the tapas, Bhagwan said, that should not be given up. So the definitive advice from Krishna, as we have seen so far, he says, this is my best in the firm opinion that yajna dhana, tapa should not be given up. And then obviously he says, how to look at this tyagaha? So now our central theme of Bhagavad Gita as we have seen is Krishnas doctrine is the tyaga.
And the tyaga defined is Sarva Karma, Falatyaga, Sarvakarma akhila. Without living any actions, whether it is desire prompted or selfless. In both cases, do not be in anticipation of a particular result.
Because as we have seen, even in doing the selfless actions, if we are bound to the Karma phala, then it is binding your ego. So Bhagavan said, perform this yajna dhana tapa but without attachment and without the expectation for the fruits of actions. attachment as ego plus egocentric Desire is attachment. I have ines and minus, then I have a desire.
So when I come in contact with an object that can satisfy the desire, Im attached. And I these days constantly talk about how we are attached to a grandchild. You know, because our ego says thats my grandchild.
And also it is enchanting. Rather its fulfilling, enchanting. So we are attached to.
So attachment is ego plus egocentric desire. And as long as that ego and egocentric desires are there, there will be an expectation for fruits of actions. So we are already worried.
She is only 20 months old. We are worried what will happen when she grow up. Will she be smart enough to do all these things? Will she be doctor or an architect? Or will she be something else? Will be artistic or athletic? Were already looking at the results of our efforts in raising her up at overload.
The Bhagavan says as long as these two are there, it will be a problem. So he said, perform all this yajnadana and tapa but without attachment in expectation for the results. So now I think Im doing the tyaga.
Im giving up some things and then feel good about it that I gave up this thing. Lets see what kind of tyaga is that. So the next three verses says Niyatasyatu sanyasah Karmano na upopady.
What should not be given up? He said: obligatory duties. Those which are the Niyata Karmas should never be given up. So we have learnt in the previous chapter there are three types of karmas.
Something which you do daily -- you are not obliging anybody by doing so. Then Niyata Karma, obligatory duties. Im a doctor, Im an architect.
Im a father, Im an employer. All those roles which Im playing, it comes with its own duties. They are Niyata Karma.
Those are my Niyata Karmas. I have to fulfill their duties. Then Naymithya Karma are special duties, special occasion, special situations.
These days, at least once in a while I find time from my routine and go see Dan in the hospital. That was not in my routine before, neither was it required that I go to MCV before Dan was admitted there. Its now a special condition which created a duty for me.
So then Namittya Karma -- Bhagavan says none of this should be given up. It is not recommended that you give up your obligatory duties. Muha Tasha Parityagaha Tama Saha Pari Kirti Taha.
Say I have given up all these duties, Niyata Karma -- Im a father but I dont want to take care of my family. I think it is binding me, so Im going to give it up -- because Im confused whether Im supposed to be doing it or not. Bhagavan says that is Tamasic Tyaga.
You have given up something, but it is Tamasic -- out of delusion, out of ignorance about your duty. If I give up something because it gives me bliss in my ignorance -- say, I dont file my taxes for five years, nobody finds out, and Im at complete bliss that I didnt pay any taxes -- thats Tamasic Tyaga. Or I dont go for voting.
This is Tamasic Tyaga, out of delusion that it is not my duty. I did not know I was supposed to file taxes? Well, I didnt file them. I did not know that my vote counts, so I didnt vote. Bhagavan says thats Tamasic Tyaga. So do all your obligated duties, but Bhagavan said, without attachment and without fixation on results.
So first thing Bhagawan said is if I give up something because of my ignorance my delusion that this is my duty its not a tiag which is going to give me any good benefits or any more liberation. It actually binds me more to the ignorance and its consequences. Ignorance of law is not an excuse. When I came from Africa.
Very first week when you start driving youre driving on a right side or left side. Your brain is not wired yet so you end up going in the wrong sense. Luckily there was no more traffic.
I said Im sorry sir but I did not know thats not an excuse my friend. Youre going to get killed if you drive on the wrong side. So bear in mind that we drive on the right side not on the wrong side.
Bhagavan said thats a Tamasic tyaga. I give up my duties out of delusion or ignorance -- that is Tamasic. Dukkham Itiyevayat Karma Kayakya Bhayat: I need to do this.
But it is too hard when it snows and there is a foot of snow in my front door. I have to keep my office entrance clear. So when the people come to my office, they dont fall.
But its too hard and theres nobody else to help me. Kayaklesa Bhayat Tyajet -- because of the fear of the pain to this body, I give up that action. Bhagavan says sakrutva rajasam tyaga.
Thats the Raja Sikhtyaga. Im giving up something I am not doing something which I should have done. I clearly know thats my duty.
To keep the entrance to my house and office clean is my duty so that nobody else can get hurt by coming to my home or my office. But out of that fear that its going to hurt my body or hurt me something, I avoid doing it. Bhagavan says it is certainly tyaga, but it is a Rajasic tyaga because it creates agitation in my mind.
Sometimes the things you dont do give you more agitation than the things you do. My standard example is calling my mother. My mother expects me to call every week.
But I end up calling every couple of months. And then what happens is when I dont call her and as the time goes by I start feeling guilty. But I dont get around calling her.
It makes me feel even more guilty. Its still I do it that day. You know, I at least called today.
I talked to her for five minutes. Okay, now Im good for a week. Well, the week passes by.
Second week, third week and I then start feeling guilty again. So this dagger of not doing my duty because its going to disrupt something Im doing here because of the time change. Obviously we have to either call her or call her in the morning or in the evening, late night.
And then thats within my clashing, my routine. And I give up that so that it does not disturb my routine. Now it gives me pleasure.
Sakrutva rajasam tyagam naivat yaga Phalam labhed. There is no benefit Im getting out of not doing that action. So it did not benefit me at all of saving that time for not calling.
It actually gave me more troubles and more agitations. Had I taken those five minutes to call her, it would have given me peace. For next five days at least.
So Bhagawan said that if youre giving up something by fear of its going to hurt you, its going to discomfort you, its going to disrupt your activities.

These verses introduce the threefold classification of tyaga that illuminates our daily choices. Tamasic tyaga is abandoning obligatory duties out of delusion or ignorance - like not filing taxes because you did not know it was required, or not voting because you think it does not matter. Rajasic tyaga is avoiding duties because they seem painful or inconvenient - the fear of physical discomfort or disruption to your routine causes you to neglect what needs to be done. The striking example given is avoiding a call to an elderly parent because it disrupts your schedule, only to suffer more from lingering guilt than the five minutes the call would have taken. Sattvic tyaga, the pure form, is performing obligatory duties because they must be done, without personal desire and without craving results.
The teaching on niyata karma (obligatory duties) is particularly relevant. These are the duties that come with our roles - as parent, professional, citizen, or community member. Krishna declares that giving up these duties out of confusion is tamasic, and avoiding them out of fear of difficulty is rajasic. Neither approach yields the benefit of true renunciation. Only when we perform our duties with the attitude karyam iti eva - simply because they must be done - do we experience sattvic action.
Ask yourself today: What obligatory duty am I currently avoiding? Is it because of genuine confusion about whether it is my responsibility (tamasic), or because it seems too hard or inconvenient (rajasic)? Identify one duty you have been postponing and perform it today with the simple understanding that it needs to be done. Notice how completing it releases the mental burden that avoiding it had created.
